title: Borel subgroups as regular-cocharacter limit subgroups
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness, connectedness and morphism properties have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-pc-morphism-conventions]. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. A smooth group is unipotent if every geometric point is a unipotent matrix in a faithful linear representation, meaning $(u-I)^n=0$ for some $n\geq1$. A reductive group is smooth and connected and has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. A torus is a group isomorphic over $F$ to $\mathbf G_m^r$, where $r\geq0$ and $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ for a commutative $F$-algebra $A$; a maximal torus is a torus subgroup maximal under inclusion. A Borel subgroup is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup. Let $G$ be reductive, $T\subseteq G$ a maximal torus, and $\Phi$ the nonzero characters of $T$ in $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, the tangent space at the identity. For $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to T$, define $P(\lambda)$ by the condition that $t\mapsto\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ extends from $\mathbf G_{m,A}$ to $\mathbf A^1_A$ for an $A$-point $g$ of $G$. Pair characters and cocharacters by $\alpha\circ\lambda(t)=t^{\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle}$. Call $\lambda$ regular if $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle\ne0$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi$. For every regular $\lambda$, the functor $P(\lambda)$ is a Borel subgroup containing $T$, and $$\operatorname{Lie}(P(\lambda))=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha.$$ Conversely every Borel subgroup containing $T$ is $P(\lambda)$ for some regular $\lambda$. The case $\Phi=\varnothing$ is allowed, with $\lambda=0$ regular and $P(0)=T=G$.

source.place: Section 13, especially Theorem 13.33 (limit subgroups); Propositions 21.29 and 21.31, Theorem 21.32 and Definition 21.35, pp.433--435.

proof.text: Fix a regular $\lambda$. Apply [lem-sfb-cocharacter-limit-smooth-structure] to $G,\lambda$, writing $P,U,Z$ for the three represented groups. By [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections], $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha$. On $\mathfrak g_\alpha$, restriction along $\lambda$ has integer weight $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle$; on $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$ it is trivial since $T$ is commutative. Regularity and the weight formulas give $\operatorname{Lie}(Z)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)$ and the asserted formula for $\operatorname{Lie}(P)$. Every $T(A)$ commutes with $\lambda$ after every scalar extension, so $T\subseteq Z\subseteq P$. The torus $T$ is smooth, $Z$ is smooth connected by the limit-group lemma, and their Lie algebras agree. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation] to the ambient smooth connected group $Z$, the one-member family $H_1=T$ (smooth connected, with $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$ spanning $\operatorname{Lie}(Z)$) and the closed subgroup $K=T$, through which the inclusion of $H_1$ factors, to obtain $Z=T$. Thus $P=U\rtimes T$.

source.place: Proposition 21.29, printed p.434, first paragraph and displayed formula; Theorem 13.33.

proof.text: The smooth unipotent group $U$ is solvable by [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable]. Because $P/U=T$ is commutative, the first scheme-theoretic commutator subgroup of $P$ is contained in $U$; its successive commutators are contained in the successive commutators of $U$. A normal series with commutative quotients for $U$ bounds this latter sequence term by term, so it terminates. Hence $P$ is solvable. It is smooth connected by step 1. Among the smooth connected solvable subgroups of $G$ containing $P$, choose $B$ of largest dimension: the set is nonempty (it contains $P$), its dimensions are nonnegative integers bounded by $\dim G$, and a strict smooth connected subgroup inclusion increases dimension, by [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. Therefore $B$ admits no larger smooth connected solvable subgroup, so is a Borel. It contains $T$.

source.place: Proposition 21.29, printed p.434, solvability and containment in a Borel; maximality made explicit.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-borel-opposite-root-dichotomy] to $B,T$. The inclusion $P\subseteq B$ implies $\operatorname{Lie}(P)\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(B)$ by the tangent-space definition (a dual-number point of $P$ is one of $B$). For each opposite pair $\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$, regularity gives exactly one positive integer pairing with $\lambda$, and step 1 puts its root space in $\operatorname{Lie}(P)$. The dichotomy says $\operatorname{Lie}(B)$ selects exactly one member of this pair and has no weights besides the selected roots and $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$. It must therefore select precisely the positive members, so $\operatorname{Lie}(P)=\operatorname{Lie}(B)$. Since $P$ is smooth connected and $B$ smooth connected, [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation] applied to the ambient group $B$, the one-member family $H_1=P$ and $K=P$ gives $P=B$. This proves the forward assertion as a subgroup-scheme statement.

source.place: Proposition 21.29, printed p.434, second paragraph; Lemma 21.28 and Proposition 10.15.

proof.text: There exists a regular cocharacter $\lambda_0$. To see this, fix $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$. Characters of this torus are integer monomials, by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality] (the split group $\mathbf G_m^r$ corresponds to $\mathbf Z^r$). For $r>0$, a root with nonzero exponent vector $(a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1})$ pairs with the cocharacter $t\mapsto(t,t^N,\ldots,t^{N^{r-1}})$ as the nonzero polynomial $a_0+a_1N+\cdots+a_{r-1}N^{r-1}$. Each has only finitely many integer zeros, so choose an integer $N$ avoiding the finite union of these zeros over $\Phi$, which is finite by [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]. This cocharacter is regular. For $r=0$ the character group is zero and $\Phi$ empty, so take $\lambda_0=0$. By steps 1--3, $B_0=P(\lambda_0)$ is a Borel containing $T$. For a given Borel $B\supseteq T$, [lem-sfb-torus-normalizer-borel-transitivity] gives $n\in G(F)$ with $nTn^{-1}=T$ and $nB_0n^{-1}=B$.

source.place: Theorem 21.32, printed pp.434--435; Corollary 17.11, printed p.355; regular-cocharacter existence underlying Corollary 21.30.

proof.text:
Set $\lambda(t)=n\lambda_0(t)n^{-1}$, a cocharacter of $T$. Conjugation by $n$ permutes the $T$-characters in $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ and preserves the character/cocharacter pairing, by [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]; hence $\lambda$ remains regular. For every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and $g\in G(A)$, write $h=n_A^{-1}gn_A$. Then
$$\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}=n_A\bigl(\lambda_0(t)h\lambda_0(t)^{-1}\bigr)n_A^{-1}.$$
Conjugation by the constant section $n_A$ is an automorphism over $\mathbf A^1_A$, so either orbit extends to $\mathbf A^1_A$ if and only if the other does. Thus $P(\lambda)(A)=n_AP(\lambda_0)(A)n_A^{-1}=B(A)$ for every $A$. This proves $P(\lambda)=B$ including nonreduced test algebras.

source.place: Theorem 21.32, printed pp.434--435; functorial conjugation calculation supplied explicitly.

proof.text: Finally, if $\Phi=\varnothing$, [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] gives $\operatorname{Lie}(G)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)$. The torus $T$ is smooth connected and $G$ is smooth connected, so [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation], applied to the one-member family $H_1=T$ and $K=T$, gives $G=T$. Every conjugation orbit for the zero cocharacter is constant, so $P(0)=G=T$ on all algebras, and $0$ is regular because the root set is empty. The same applies to the trivial group.

source.place: Proposition 21.29 and Theorem 21.32, rootless case, made explicit.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 21.29 and Theorem 21.32, printed pp.433--435, with their inputs Theorem 13.33, Example 14.13, Lemma 21.28, Proposition 10.15 and Corollary 17.11. The all-algebra conjugation calculation and regular-cocharacter choice are written out.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q137-54fa226ef (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: I read the whole item, all three new nodes and every cited statement against Milne iAG2017: Prop 10.15 and Cor 10.17 (p.191), Thm 13.33(a)-(e) (pp.265-266), Ex 14.13, Thm 21.11(b),(c), Lemma 21.28, Prop 21.29 and Thm 21.32 (pp.433-435). Step by step: (1) Z=T by regularity and the limit-group Lie formulas, and Lie(P) is T plus the positive roots. (2) P is solvable because U is solvable and P/U=T is commutative; a Borel B containing P is chosen of maximal dimension. (3) The opposite-root dichotomy gives Lie B = Lie P, so P=B. (4) A regular cocharacter (t,t^N,...) exists, and the normalizer-transitivity node supplies n. (5) Conjugation by n works on every test algebra and keeps the cocharacter regular. (6) With no roots, G=T and P(0)=G. This follows Milne 21.29/21.32 correctly, with no characteristic restriction. There is no cycle, and every citation is in unit sk-thm-sf-ctf-stability, so there is no off-unit tool use. The two new nodes I keep, cocharacter-limit-smooth-structure (13.33+14.13) and borel-opposite-root-dichotomy (21.28+21.11), are true and are not restatements of the item; I tested them on lambda=0, a central GL_2 cocharacter, SL_2 upper and lower Borels, and characteristic 2.
